newsitem.title: Russia: Yeltsin eyes union with Belarus but liberals worry.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin eyes union with Belarus but liberals worry.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin plans to forge closer ties with Russia's Slav ally Belarus this week, but liberal leaders say he is moving too fast and not consulting the Russian people enough.

Yeltsin and Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko are due to sign a document in Moscow on Wednesday which officials say will help bring their two countries closer together. Details of the document have not been announced.

Their drive for rapid integration contrasts with the mood of other members of the loose Commonwealth of Independent States who appeared divided on many issues at a summit last Friday of the 12-nation group formed on the ashes of the Soviet Union.

"Yes, the question really arose at our session, how can we move forward? Nevertheless, we later reached the common conclusion that the Commonwealth was necessary," Yeltsin said after the Moscow summit.
The secrecy with which Wednesday's agreement has been drawn up has angered liberal leaders in Moscow who say the Russian people have not been consulted properly.

"It would be an unprecedented event to try to ratify such an agreement in parliament without any kind of consideration of this document," Grigory Yavlinksy, leader of the liberal Yaboko bloc, told NTV commercial television.
Former acting prime minster Yegor Gaidar said: "The least that should have been done was to publish it (the document), consider it calmly and not rush into signing it."
They and other Russian liberals are also concerned by Lukashenko's authoritarian methods, including the decision last week to expel an NTV correspondent from Belarus.
About 30 protesters tried to demonstrate for media freedom outside the Belarussian embassy in Moscow on Sunday but police prevented them from doing so. Several people were detained.
Yeltsin, 66, appears to believe forging better ties with Belarus is a trump card because many Russians are nostalgic for the Soviet Union which fell apart in 1991.
Kremlin aide Sergei Shakhrai said in a television interview on Sunday that union with Belarus would be in Russia's interests and would not jeopardise its decision-making powers.

The drive for integration with Russia's less wealthy western neighbour of about 10 million people could also deflect attention from the economic problems which prompted nationwide protests last Thursday and play into his political foes' hands.

Last Thursday's demonstrations, though apparently attended by fewer people thant the trade union organisers had expected, signalled discontent with policies that have left many people unpaid for months.
An opinion poll published on Sunday showed 68 percent of respondents believed recent events had shown that the country is in general heading up a dead-end street.

The poll, carried out by the independent research group VTsIOM and published in the weekly newspaper Interfax-Argumenty i Fakty, showed only 14 percent of the 1,630 respondents thought Russia was going the right way. Eighteen percent were undecided.

The poll, conducted from March 14 to 19, also showed that Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov would win most support if a presidential election were held immediately and Yeltsin did not run -- he cannot seek a third term under the constitution.

Zyuganov won 18 percent support and tough-talking Alexander Lebed, Yeltsin's ousted security adviser and now a critic of his policies, was second with 15 percent backing. Yavlinsky trailed in third place with six percent support.
